title: Shteli Kherkher, the Mountain Guardian
summary: A nature spirit of the Hindu Kush mountains who protects the wild animals and punishes hunters who kill for sport.
full_text:
In the high passes of the Hindu Kush, where the snow never melts and the wind cuts like a blade, there lives a guardian of the wild places. The Shteli Kherkher is a being of stone and ice, his skin the color of granite, his hair like frozen waterfalls. He moves silently across the slopes, watching everything. He is the protector of the markhor, the snow leopard, the ibex. No hunter can take game from his mountains without his permission.

The Shteli Kherkher does not hate humans. He understands that men must eat, that families must be fed. A hunter who prays before the hunt, who takes only one animal and uses every part, who thanks the mountain for its bounty, will find the Shteli Kherkher's blessing upon him. His aim will be true, his path safe, his return swift. But the hunter who kills for glory, who leaves carcasses to rot, who hunts the pregnant and the young, will never see the Shteli Kherkher coming. He will simply step on a loose stone, or his rifle will jam, or the fog will descend and he will lose his way. Some say the Shteli Kherkher pushes men off cliffs, but that is not true. He merely removes his protection, and the mountain does the rest.

A famous tale tells of a wealthy merchant from Kabul who came to the mountains to hunt markhor for their horns. He laughed at the warnings of the local shepherds. Within two days, his guide had vanished, his horse had gone lame, and he was lost in a blizzard. He stumbled for three days before collapsing. When he woke, he was in a shepherd's hut. 'The Shteli Kherkher spared you,' the shepherd said. 'He saw that your heart was not entirely black. Go home and do not return.' The merchant returned to Kabul and became a patron of conservation, using his wealth to protect the very animals he had once hunted.

The Shteli Kherkher is still there, in the high places. When the mountain goats gather on a ridge and look back at the valley below, they are listening to him.
moral: The mountain provides for those who respect it.
source: Afghan oral tradition, Central Asian folklore

title: Peri, the Winged Spirit of Afghanistan
summary: Beautiful winged spirits who dwell between heaven and earth, the Peri are benevolent beings who guide lost souls and protect sacred springs.
full_text:
Of all the spirits that inhabit the Afghan landscape, the Peri are the most beautiful and the most mysterious. They are not angels, for they are not made of divine light. They are not djinn, for they are not made of fire. They are something in between, beings of gentle air and soft light, with wings like a dragonfly's but shimmering with all the colors of dawn. The Peri live in the high valleys, near clear springs and ancient trees. They are drawn to beauty and purity.

The Peri are helpers. They guide lost children home. They lead travelers to water. They whisper wisdom to poets and musicians. A young man who plays the rebab well may find his music suddenly elevated, his fingers moving with a grace he did not know he possessed. That is the Peri touching his hand. A woman weaving a carpet may see colors in her mind that she has never seen before. That is the Peri inspiring her.

But the Peri cannot abide cruelty or ugliness of spirit. A warlord who terrorized a village in the Panjshir Valley found his victories turning to ash. His weapons rusted overnight. His men deserted him. His dreams were filled with the faces of the winged ones, weeping. He died alone, in a ditch, forgotten. The villagers said the Peri had turned their faces from him, and without their blessing, no man could prosper.

A story from Herat tells of a Peri who fell in love with a human musician. She visited him every night for a year, dancing to his music. He grew famous, wealthy, sought after. But fame made him arrogant. He stopped playing for joy and played only for gold. The Peri stopped coming. He lost his gift, his fortune, and finally his mind, wandering the streets of Herat, calling for his winged muse. The lesson is clear: the Peri give freely, but they despise those who sell their gifts for profit.

To this day, Afghan musicians leave a small offering of bread and rosewater before performing, hoping a Peri will listen.
moral: True art is a gift from the divine and cannot be bought or sold.
source: Afghan oral tradition, Persian/Central Asian folklore

title: Div (Daeva), the Demon of the Waste
summary: A powerful demon from Zoroastrian tradition who brings drought, disease, and despair to the people of the Afghan highlands.
full_text:
Before the Prophet brought the word of God to Afghanistan, before the Buddhist monks carved their giant Buddhas into the cliffs of Bamiyan, there was the ancient faith of the Magi. The Zoroastrians knew the Div as one of the daevas, the demons who served Angra Mainyu, the spirit of darkness. The Div is no petty trickster. He is a lord of destruction, a bringer of drought and plague. His body is massive, covered in coarse hair, with horns that curve like a ram's and eyes that burn with the fire of the abyss.

The Div does not lurk in shadows. He rules the wastelands, the desert stretches where nothing grows, the mountain passes where travelers freeze. He sends dust storms to blind the righteous and famine to test the faithful. The only way to withstand the Div is through unity and prayer. A village united against his influence can weather any storm. A village divided will be picked apart, one family at a time.

A mullah in Badakhshan once encountered the Div in a dream. The demon offered him wealth, power, the love of the most beautiful woman in the world, in exchange for a single prayer spoken backward. The mullah refused. 'Even in my dreams, I will not serve you,' he said. The Div howled and vanished. The mullah woke to find his hands covered in scratches, as if he had been fighting something in his sleep. But he had won. The villagers who heard his story took strength from it, and their harvest that year was the best in a decade.

The Div is still out there, in the dry places, waiting for a moment of weakness. He is the shadow that falls when faith falters, the voice that whispers that hope is a lie. To defeat him, the old say, you need only remember that light always returns after darkness.
moral: Faith and unity are the only shields against despair.
source: Afghan oral tradition, Zoroastrian/Central Asian folklore

title: Div-e Sepid, the White Demon
summary: A legendary white demon from Persian epic tradition, the Div-e Sepid is a monstrous being of immense strength who terrorized the heroes of old.
full_text:
Among the demons of Afghan and Persian legend, none is more famous than the Div-e Sepid, the White Demon. He appears in the Shahnameh, the great epic of Persian kings, and his story has been told in the mountains of Afghanistan for a thousand years. The Div-e Sepid is a giant, white as snow, with a face that is never clearly seen because looking upon it is death. He lives in a dark cave atop Mount Damavand, surrounded by the bones of those who tried to defeat him.

Unlike many demons who tempt and trick, the Div-e Sepid is a brute force of nature. He does not offer bargains. He does not whisper lies. He simply destroys. His strength is such that he can uproot trees, throw boulders across valleys, and crush iron with his bare hands. He commands an army of lesser demons, and together they raid villages, steal cattle, and carry off women. For generations, the people of the region lived in terror of the White Demon.

The hero Rostam eventually faced the Div-e Sepid. The battle lasted a day and a night. The White Demon struck Rostam with a boulder that would have crushed any ordinary man. But Rostam was no ordinary man. He was a son of the mountains, fed on the milk of wild goats, trained by the greatest warriors of the age. He dodged, he struck, he wore the demon down. Finally, he drove his dagger into the White Demon's heart. The body crumbled to ash, and the ash scattered on the wind. But some say the Div-e Sepid cannot truly die. He reforms in his cave whenever the world becomes cruel enough to call him back.

The White Demon remains a symbol of the struggle between order and chaos. When Afghanistan faces its darkest hours, the old storytellers say, the Div-e Sepid stirs in his mountain. But so does the spirit of Rostam, in the hearts of those who refuse to bow to tyranny.
moral: No tyrant is so strong that courage cannot defeat him.
source: Afghan oral tradition, Persian epic folklore
